fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when I started my PhD at MIT with Regina Barzilay, this was around 2012, 2013, and the dominant paradigm in NLP at the time was still very much about treating text as the whole universe. You'd have a corpus, you'd annotate it, you'd train a model to predict labels, and the entire feedback loop lived inside the text itself. And I remember feeling a bit dissatisfied with that, because that's not how humans acquire language at all. A kid doesn't learn what "hot" means by reading a million sentences containing the word "hot." They touch the stove.

So the question I kept coming back to was: what does it actually mean for a system to understand a sentence? And one answer I found compelling was that understanding means being able to act on it. If I tell you "the key is under the mat," you understand that sentence if you can go lift the mat and get the key. The meaning is cashed out in terms of consequences in some environment.

That's what pulled me toward text-based games, actually. Those old interactive fiction games, where the whole world is described to you in text and you type commands back. They were this beautiful testbed, because the language was rich and natural, but there was also an environment with real state and real rewards. The game would tell you whether your interpretation was right, not by a human annotator, but by whether the door opened. And this was right when deep reinforcement learning was starting to work, the Atari results had just come out, so it felt like the pieces were lining up. You could train an agent to map from language to actions, and the reward signal would do the work that annotation used to do.

I think what really hooked me was that it reframed the problem. Instead of asking "can the model predict this label," you're asking "can the model use language to get something done." And that felt like a much more honest definition of understanding. It's a thread that's stayed with me, honestly, through the work on using external evidence for information extraction, and even into thinking about agents today. The grounding question never really went away for me, it just kept finding new environments.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes using deep reinforcement learning to train agents to map language to actions, with environmental rewards teaching the system whether its language understanding was correct.

opus-5.5.text:
Guest: Honestly, it started from a kind of dissatisfaction with how we were doing NLP at the time. When I started my PhD at MIT with Regina Barzilay, most of the field was about taking a big annotated corpus, training a model to predict some label, like a parse tree or a sentiment tag, and measuring accuracy on a held-out set. That works, but it always felt a bit disconnected from what language is actually *for*. We don't use language to produce parse trees. We use it to get things done, to tell someone how to do something, to coordinate, to pass on knowledge.

So I kept coming back to this question: what does it mean for a machine to understand a sentence? One reasonable answer is that it understands if it can act on it correctly. If I tell you "go to the kitchen and grab the key on the table," you understand that sentence if you end up in the kitchen holding the key. That framing of meaning tied to behavior in some environment was really appealing to me because it gives you a much richer signal than a static label.

Around that time deep reinforcement learning was having its moment. The DQN results on Atari had just come out, and it was exciting to see agents learning directly from raw pixels and reward. My thought was, why not do the same thing with language? That led to our work on text-based games, the old interactive fiction games like Zork, where the entire world is described to you in text and you have to type commands to make progress. They're a great testbed because the agent has to understand the descriptions well enough to act, and the only feedback it gets is whether it's making progress in the game. Nobody hands it labeled examples of what each sentence means.

The other piece I found compelling was the reverse direction: language as a way to make learning easier. Humans rarely learn a new task from scratch through pure trial and error. We read the manual, someone gives us advice, we look things up. So a lot of my later PhD work asked whether an agent could read text about an environment, like a description of what different objects do, and use that to learn faster or transfer to a new environment it's never seen. Even then that felt like a really important capability, because pure RL is incredibly sample inefficient, and language is this compressed store of human knowledge sitting right there.

So it was a mix of the philosophical question, what is understanding, and the practical one, how do we build agents that learn the way people do, by leveraging language rather than ignoring it. That thread has stayed with me, even through the language modeling work, which in some ways came at the problem from the opposite side.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly connects reinforcement learning with language understanding, describing agents learning from language in text-based games and understanding sentences by acting on them correctly.

fable-5.text:
Yeah, so this goes back to when I started my PhD at MIT with Regina Barzilay, around 2012, 2013. At the time, most of NLP was what I'd call text-to-text processing — you take some text in, you produce some annotation or some other text out, whether that's parsing or translation or summarization. And the thing that kept nagging at me was that language doesn't actually exist in a vacuum like that. When humans use language, it's connected to the world — we use it to get things done, to change someone's beliefs, to coordinate actions. The meaning of words comes from their consequences, not just from their co-occurrence with other words.

There was actually some work in Regina's lab just before I joined that really captured my imagination — this idea of an agent reading the manual for a game like Civilization and using that text to actually play the game better. That was a lightbulb moment for me, because it flipped the usual setup: instead of language understanding being the end goal, language becomes a means to an end. You can measure understanding by whether the agent does better in the world after reading. That felt like a much more honest test of comprehension than matching some annotated label.

So that's what pulled me toward text-based games as a research vehicle. Games like the old Infocom adventures — Zork and so on — are this wonderful sandbox, because the entire world is rendered in language. The observations are text, your actions are text, and you get a reward signal from the game. So you can ask: can an agent learn representations of language purely from interaction, from trial and error? We ended up combining deep learning with reinforcement learning for this, which at the time — this was around 2015 — was still a pretty unusual combination in NLP.

And honestly, part of the draw was just a stubborn belief that this was where things had to go eventually. If you want machines that actually assist people — that follow instructions, that take actions, that learn from feedback — you need language grounded in behavior. It's funny looking back, because that thread of agents that read and act, which felt pretty fringe during my PhD, is now sort of at the center of everything.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes combining reinforcement learning with deep learning so agents learn language representations through interaction and trial and error, grounding language understanding in behavior.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, it came out of a kind of dissatisfaction. When I started my PhD at MIT with Regina Barzilay, a lot of NLP was essentially pattern matching over text — you'd build a parser or a classifier, you'd get a number on a benchmark, and the model never had to care what any of the words actually referred to. And that bothered me, because the thing that makes language interesting is that it's *about* something. If I tell you "the door on your left is locked," that sentence is only meaningful because it changes what you do next.

So I got very interested in setups where you could actually measure whether understanding happened — where the only way to succeed at a task is to have correctly interpreted the text. We did some work on reading instruction manuals for games, Civilization in particular, where the manual tells you things like which units counter which, and you can check whether the agent's play improves because it read the document. Then text-based games became a really nice sandbox, because the entire world is language — the observations are text, the actions are text, and there's a reward signal telling you whether you got it right.

And the deeper bet, which I think has mostly been borne out, was that grounding isn't just a nice-to-have for robotics or embodied agents. It's where the pressure comes from that forces a model to actually build representations of the world rather than of the corpus.

r001.rationale: The response mentions text-based games with actions and reward signals, but it never clearly states that reinforcement learning was used to teach systems language understanding.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I came at it from a fairly practical frustration. When I started my PhD at MIT, most NLP work treated language as text in, label out. You'd train a model on a big annotated corpus and it would learn statistical patterns, but it never had to *do* anything with what it read. To me that felt like it was missing the point of language. People use language to get things done, to coordinate, to give instructions, to describe how the world works.

So I got interested in settings where understanding language has a measurable consequence. If a model reads a description of a game or an environment, can it use that to act better? If the text says "lava is dangerous," does the agent actually learn to avoid lava faster? That gives you a much cleaner signal for whether the model understood than asking it to match a human label.

My advisor, Regina Barzilay, was very supportive of that direction. It was also a natural meeting point with reinforcement learning, since the agent's reward tells you whether it grounded the language correctly. Early on, a lot of the work was on text-based games and on using language to help agents transfer to new environments.

Looking back, a lot of what I've worked on since, including language models and agents, grew out of that same question: how do you connect words to something beyond other words?

r001.rationale: The response explicitly connects language grounding with reinforcement learning, describing agents learning from language to act better and using rewards to determine whether they grounded the language correctly.

haiku-5.5.text: I think it came from noticing how much language work at the time happened on static text with no connection to what the words referred to. A model could predict the next word well and still have no sense that "pick up the key" means something different when the key is on the table versus already in your hand. Text-based games made that gap concrete for me. The world was small enough to reason about, but the language only made sense if you acted on it and saw what changed. That led me to ask whether an agent could learn what instructions meant from rewards for doing the right thing, and whether those grounded representations would carry over to new situations. The transfer question ended up mattering more to me than I expected.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes learning instruction meanings from rewards for taking the correct actions, which communicates using reinforcement learning to ground and understand language.

astra-6.text: What drew me in was the question of how language connects to the world. We can build systems that recognize patterns in text, but how do we get them to connect those words to things they can observe or actions they can take? If you give a system an instruction, understanding it should mean being able to do something useful with it. That connection also gives you a way to learn: you take an action, see what happens, and revise your understanding. I found that interplay between language, action, and learning really compelling.

r001.rationale: The response mentions taking actions, observing outcomes, and revising understanding, but it does not explicitly describe using reinforcement learning to teach systems to understand language.

That makes grounding a really interesting learning problem. If I tell a system to pick something up or move somewhere, it has to connect those words to objects, actions, and changes in its environment. And the feedback gives it another way to learn what the language means. That connection between language, learning, and decision-making was what drew me toward it.
